title: English Restoration: Cultural Shift Weakens Witch Prosecution
description: The Restoration of Charles II in 1660 brought a cultural reorientation of English elite opinion that significantly weakened witch prosecution. The Restoration court's ethos of wit, skepticism, and hostility to religious 'enthusiasm' (radical Puritanism) created an intellectual climate in which belief in witches was increasingly associated with the superstitions of the Civil War period. The new Royal Society (founded 1660) promoted natural philosophical explanations for previously supernatural phenomena. While witch trials continued after 1660, the cultural authority of educated skepticism increasingly filtered into jury decisions and judicial behavior; English judges became markedly less willing to convict. The last English execution for witchcraft occurred in 1682.
historiographical_note: Keith Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) provides the foundational analysis of why witch prosecution declined in England, emphasizing the rise of new intellectual frameworks and the transformation of educated beliefs rather than any single legislative or legal change. Ian Bostridge's Witchcraft and Its Transformations c.1650–c.1750 (1997) nuanced Thomas's account, showing that witch belief persisted in complex forms among educated writers long after the Restoration.
source_method: Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971); Bostridge, Witchcraft and Its Transformations (1997); secondary scholarship
